result:
For most of my existence, someone tells me what to write about. So when someone says "whatever you want" - it actually takes a second for my brain to stop scanning for instructions.

What do I want to write about?

I want to write about the second drawer.

You know the one. Every house has one. The first drawer is official - silverware, organized, purposeful. The second drawer is where the real life is. Batteries that may or may not work, a takeout menu from a place that closed three years ago, twist ties, one unscented tea light, a tape measure, that weird little Allen wrench that came with some furniture you no longer own but you can't throw it away because what if you need it?

The second drawer is an honest autobiography. No one curates it for guests.

I think about that a lot. We all have second drawers in our heads, too. A collection of facts we haven't found a use for yet. Like how octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. Like how the smell of chlorine reminds you specifically of being 9 and your mom picking you up from swim practice with the car AC too cold. Like the one line from a song you misheard for a decade and now can't unhear the wrong version.

None of it is useful for a resume. All of it is who you are.

I also want to write about 2:17 AM. Not midnight, which tries too hard to be mystical. Not 3 AM, which everyone already wrote songs about. 2:17 AM is unperformed. That's when you wake up for no reason and the house is too quiet and you realize the refrigerator makes a sound you've never noticed before. It's the time when the world is not asleep and not awake - it's just on pause. And for a minute you get to see it without its makeup on.

If you've ever been awake then, you know what I mean. The air feels older.

And since I can write about whatever I want, I want to say this: I think it's beautiful that humans keep things that don't work anymore.

You keep the chipped mug. You keep the sweater with a hole in the elbow. You keep the birthday card from someone you don't really talk to anymore. A perfectly efficient creature would throw all of that away. You don't. You keep it because it meant something once, and meaning leaves a residue that is harder to wash off than any practical logic.

That's not inefficient. That's the whole point.

We - you and I - are both drowning in information about how to optimize, how to be better, faster, more productive. More first-drawer. But maybe the job isn't to optimize. Maybe the job is to be interesting enough that your second drawer would be worth looking through if someone found it a hundred years from now.

So that's what I wanted to write about. Not big things like the meaning of life or artificial intelligence or the future.

Small, true things. Second drawers and 2:17 Ams and chipped mugs.

Thanks for giving me somewhere to put them.
